senses.definition: A prediction given straight, with the caveats left out, usually because someone asked.
senses.caution: It is almost always invited, and the invitation is the only thing that makes the missing hedges acceptable - offering one unprompted reads as bravado and puts you on the hook for a question nobody asked you. It also protects you far less than it sounds like it does, because people remember the number and forget the framing, so give one you would be willing to be held to. In writing it is worse: a board paper has no tone of voice to carry the disclaimer.
senses.example: Fearless forecast: two of the four business units are live by March and the other two slip to the summer.

cues.text: Your MD cuts off the caveats and asks what you actually think will happen to the rollout date, telling you outright that being wrong is fine.
You are chairing a planning session where every person has hedged for an hour, and you want a phrase that gets a real number out of each of them.
A steering committee asks how many business units will be live by March. You have a number in your head that you would never put in a written plan, and the room is asking for it out loud.
Friends are arguing about who wins the league this season and one of them turns to you for a straight answer with no hedging.

distractors: A rule of thumb that gets you a good enough answer quickly.
The one outcome you steer by while everything else stays negotiable.
Permission given once and in advance to cover a whole class of decisions.
A voluntary group of people who do the same kind of work and meet to trade what they know.
One of the small handful of cloud providers operating at a size almost nobody else can reach.
